column3: Now when it was decided that we should sail to Italy, they handed over both Paul and some other prisoners to a centurion named Julius from the Augustan cohort.
And boarding an Adramyttian ship that was about to sail to places along the coast of Asia, we put to sea, with Aristarchus, a Macedonian from Thessalonica, being with us.
On the next day we landed at Sidon, and Julius, treating Paul kindly, allowed him to go to his friends to receive care.
And putting out to sea from there, we sailed under the shelter of Cyprus because the winds were contrary.
And sailing across the open sea along Cilicia and Pamphylia, we came to Myra in Lycia.
And there the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing to Italy and put us aboard it.
For many days we sailed slowly and with difficulty came opposite Cnidus. Since the wind did not allow us to go farther, we sailed under the shelter of Crete near Salmone.
And sailing along it with difficulty, we came to a certain place called Fair Havens, near which was the city of Lasea.
Now when considerable time had passed and the voyage was already dangerous because even the Fast had already passed, Paul began advising them,
saying, “Men, I perceive that the voyage is about to be with injury and much loss, not only of the cargo and ship but also of our lives.”
But the centurion was persuaded by the pilot and the shipowner rather than by the things Paul was saying.

And since the harbor was unsuitable for wintering, the majority gave advice to put out to sea from there, if somehow they might reach Phoenix to spend the winter, a harbor of Crete facing southwest and northwest.
When a south wind blew gently, thinking they had obtained their purpose, they weighed anchor and sailed closely along Crete.
But not long afterward a violent wind called the Northeaster rushed down from the island.
And when the ship was caught and unable to face into the wind, we gave way and were driven along.
Running under the shelter of a small island called Cauda, we were barely able to secure the lifeboat.
After hoisting it up, they used supports to undergird the ship. And fearing that they might run aground on the Syrtis, they lowered the gear and thus were driven along.
And since we were being violently storm-tossed, on the next day they began throwing cargo overboard,
and on the third day they threw the ship’s equipment overboard with their own hands.
Now when neither sun nor stars appeared for many days, and no small storm was pressing upon us, all hope that we would be saved was finally being taken away.
And after they had gone a long time without food, Paul stood in their midst and said, “Men, you should have listened to me and not put out from Crete and gained this injury and loss.
And now I urge you to take courage, for there will be no loss of life among you, but only of the ship.
For this night an angel of the God whose I am and whom I serve stood beside me,
saying, ‘Do not be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar, and look, God has graciously given you all those sailing with you.’
Therefore take courage, men, for I believe God that it will happen in this way, just as it has been spoken to me.
But we must run aground on some island.”
Now when the fourteenth night came, as we were being driven about in the Adriatic Sea, around midnight the sailors began to suspect that some land was approaching them.
And taking soundings, they found twenty fathoms. A little farther on, taking soundings again, they found fifteen fathoms.
And fearing that we might run aground somewhere on rocky places, they threw four anchors from the stern and were praying for day to come.
But as the sailors were seeking to escape from the ship and had lowered the lifeboat into the sea under pretense of intending to lay out anchors from the bow,
Paul said to the centurion and the soldiers, “Unless these men remain in the ship, you cannot be saved.”
Then the soldiers cut away the ropes of the lifeboat and allowed it to fall away.
Now until day was about to come, Paul was urging everyone to take food, saying, “Today is the fourteenth day you have continued waiting without food, taking nothing.
Therefore I urge you to take some food, for this is for your survival, since not a hair from the head of any of you will be lost.”
And after saying these things, he took bread, gave thanks to God before everyone, broke it, and began to eat.
Then they all became encouraged and themselves also took food.
Now we were in all two hundred seventy-six souls on the ship.
And after being satisfied with food, they began lightening the ship by throwing the wheat into the sea.
When day came, they did not recognize the land, but they noticed a certain bay with a beach, on which they planned, if possible, to drive the ship ashore.
And casting off the anchors, they left them in the sea, at the same time loosening the bands of the rudders. And raising the foresail to the wind, they headed toward the beach.
But striking a place where two seas met, they ran the vessel aground, and the bow stuck fast and remained immovable, but the stern was being broken apart by the force of the waves.
Now the soldiers’ plan was to kill the prisoners so that none might swim away and escape.
But the centurion, wanting to save Paul, prevented them from their purpose and ordered those able to swim to jump overboard first and go to the land,
and the rest, some on planks and others on pieces from the ship. And in this way it happened that everyone was brought safely to the land.
